A separate risk concerns whether the company, once goods are produced, can actually sell them, considering pricing and market penetration. Which two risks does this respectively describe?
opts: Marketing Risk, then Production Risk
Production Risk, then Marketing Risk
Supply Risk, then Demand Risk
Production Risk, then Demand Risk
questionBank.ans: Production Risk, then Marketing Risk
questionBank.exp: Completing production is Production Risk; selling the finished output is Marketing Risk. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute Supply/Demand Risk instead.

questionBank.q: One risk concerns uncertainty in accessing the inputs a company needs for production, considering the number of major suppliers and substitute availability. A separate risk concerns whether the company can generate enough customer patronage for its output, considering competitive advantage and rivalry intensity. Which two risks does this respectively describe?
opts: Demand Risk, then Supply Risk
Supply Risk, then Demand Risk
Business Risk, then Collection Risk
Supply Risk, then Collection Risk
questionBank.ans: Supply Risk, then Demand Risk
questionBank.exp: Uncertainty in accessing inputs is Supply Risk; uncertainty in generating patronage for output is Demand Risk. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute unrelated risks.

questionBank.q: An SME wholesale distributor sources inventory from multiple domestic and international suppliers and extends 30-day credit terms to a wide base of retail and e-commerce customers. A review flags that several customers have recently been paying well past their 30-day terms. Which risk in the operating cycle most directly requires closer attention here?
opts: Supply Risk, since multiple suppliers are involved
Collection Risk, since receivables are not being converted to cash on schedule
Production Risk, since the company does not manufacture its own goods
Business Risk, since the company operates across multiple sales channels
questionBank.ans: Collection Risk, since receivables are not being converted to cash on schedule
questionBank.exp: Customers paying well past agreed credit terms is a direct signal of Collection Risk, tied to customer credibility and credit terms management. The other risks are present in the business generally but are not what this specific late-payment pattern signals.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is one of the six risks in the operating cycle of borrowers listed in the material?
opts: Regulatory Risk
Supply Risk
Currency Risk
Reputational Risk
questionBank.ans: Supply Risk
questionBank.exp: Supply Risk is one of the six listed risks, alongside Business, Demand, Production, Marketing, and Collection Risk. The other options are not among the six risks named in this section.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is one of the four steps in the Credit Risk Management process?
opts: Negotiation
Monitoring
Litigation
Marketing
questionBank.ans: Monitoring
questionBank.exp: Monitoring is one of the four steps in Credit Risk Management, alongside Identification, Measurement, and Control. The other options are not part of this four-step process.

questionBank.q: A bank requires collateral on a facility and considers this sufficient on its own to control credit risk exposure, without setting any lending limits or diversifying its portfolio. Based on the material's listed control methods, is this approach adequate?
opts: Yes, collateral alone is described as fully sufficient for control
No, collateral is only one of several listed control methods
Yes, but only for facilities below the bank's largest exposure limit
No, because collateral is not actually a recognized control method
questionBank.ans: No, collateral is only one of several listed control methods
questionBank.exp: Requiring collateral is listed as one control method among several, alongside setting lending limits and diversifying the portfolio — relying on it alone leaves other control methods unused. The other options overstate collateral's sufficiency or deny it is a control method at all.

questionBank.q: A bank charges a higher interest rate and requires additional collateral from a borrower assessed as higher-risk, to compensate for the increased likelihood of default. Which credit risk management method is being applied?
opts: Portfolio Diversification
Risk-Based Pricing
Early Warning Systems
Regulatory Compliance
questionBank.ans: Risk-Based Pricing
questionBank.exp: Adjusting interest rates and terms based on perceived credit risk is Risk-Based Pricing. The other methods involve spreading exposure across the portfolio, detecting deteriorating credit quality, and meeting regulatory requirements respectively.

questionBank.q: A bank uses credit default swaps to transfer the risk of a borrower's default to another market participant. Which credit risk management method is being applied?
opts: Credit Scoring Models
Credit Risk Transfer
Collateralization
Stress Testing and Scenario Analysis
questionBank.ans: Credit Risk Transfer
questionBank.exp: Using instruments like credit default swaps to transfer default risk to other market participants is Credit Risk Transfer. The other methods involve statistical scoring, pledged assets, and simulating adverse conditions respectively.

questionBank.q: A bank monitors delinquency rates, default rates, and credit migration trends across its loan portfolio specifically to catch deteriorating credit quality before it becomes a larger problem. Which credit risk management method is this, and what should the bank do upon spotting such warning signs?
opts: Stress Testing, and wait for the next scheduled stress test before acting
Early Warning Systems, and act promptly rather than waiting for full default to occur
Credit Risk Transfer, and immediately transfer the exposure regardless of severity
Portfolio Diversification, and take no action since diversification already covers this risk
questionBank.ans: Early Warning Systems, and act promptly rather than waiting for full default to occur
questionBank.exp: Monitoring these indicators to detect deteriorating credit quality is the purpose of Early Warning Systems, and the point of such systems is to prompt timely action rather than waiting for a full default. The other options misidentify the method or suggest an inappropriately passive or extreme response.

questionBank.q: One credit risk management method spreads a bank's lending across various industries, geographic regions, and counterparties to reduce concentration risk. A separate method sets maximum exposure levels for individual borrowers, counterparties, and portfolios. Which two methods does this respectively describe?
opts: Credit Limits and Exposure Management, then Portfolio Diversification
Portfolio Diversification, then Credit Limits and Exposure Management
Collateralization, then Portfolio Diversification
Portfolio Diversification, then Stress Testing and Scenario Analysis
questionBank.ans: Portfolio Diversification, then Credit Limits and Exposure Management
questionBank.exp: Spreading exposure across industries, regions, and counterparties is Portfolio Diversification; setting maximum exposure levels is Credit Limits and Exposure Management. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute unrelated methods.

questionBank.q: A bank's credit risk processes are otherwise sound, but it has fallen behind on adhering to regulatory guidelines for loan classification and reporting. Based on the material's listed credit risk management methods, what gap does this represent?
opts: A gap in Credit Scoring Models, since classification is a scoring function
A gap in Regulatory Compliance, a distinct listed method in its own right
No real gap, since regulatory guidelines are optional for internal risk processes
A gap in Collateralization, since classification depends on pledged assets
questionBank.ans: A gap in Regulatory Compliance, a distinct listed method in its own right
questionBank.exp: Regulatory Compliance — adherence to loan classification, provisioning, and reporting guidelines — is a distinct listed credit risk management method, so falling behind on it is a real, specific gap even if other processes are sound. The other options misattribute the gap or wrongly treat compliance as optional.

questionBank.q: Which credit risk management method involves thoroughly evaluating a borrower's financial statements, cash flow, and collateral, guided by established underwriting standards?
opts: Credit Risk Transfer
Credit Assessment and Underwriting
Stress Testing and Scenario Analysis
Early Warning Systems
questionBank.ans: Credit Assessment and Underwriting
questionBank.exp: Thorough evaluation of creditworthiness guided by underwriting standards is Credit Assessment and Underwriting. The other methods involve transferring risk to third parties, simulating adverse scenarios, and detecting deteriorating credit quality respectively.

questionBank.q: How is Expected Loss (EL) described in the material?
opts: The maximum possible loss a lender could suffer under any circumstance
The average loss a lender anticipates from a loan portfolio over a specific period
The loss a lender suffers only after a borrower is declared bankrupt
A loss figure that excludes any consideration of collateral
questionBank.ans: The average loss a lender anticipates from a loan portfolio over a specific period
questionBank.exp: Expected Loss represents the average loss a lender anticipates from a loan portfolio over a specific period. The other options describe a worst-case scenario, a narrower trigger event, or misstate what EL considers.

questionBank.q: Why does the material caution against relying solely on Expected Loss for provisioning?
opts: Because Expected Loss is always calculated incorrectly by lenders
Because Unexpected Losses can be significant, especially during economic downturns
Because Expected Loss does not require any historical data to calculate
Because regulators have banned the use of Expected Loss entirely
questionBank.ans: Because Unexpected Losses can be significant, especially during economic downturns
questionBank.exp: Unexpected Losses can be significant, especially during economic downturns, which is why relying solely on Expected Loss for provisioning is risky. The other options misstate the material's reasoning or invent claims not made.

questionBank.q: A lender sets aside provisions based only on its calculated Expected Loss and does not maintain any additional capital buffer for unexpected losses. Based on the material's discussion, is this approach adequate?
opts: Yes, since Expected Loss already accounts for all possible loss scenarios
No, since regulators require capital buffers to absorb unexpected losses beyond Expected Loss
Yes, since Unexpected Losses only matter for retail, not corporate, lending
No, but only during periods of economic growth
questionBank.ans: No, since regulators require capital buffers to absorb unexpected losses beyond Expected Loss
questionBank.exp: Regulators require banks to hold capital buffers that can absorb unexpected losses, because relying solely on Expected Loss provisioning is risky, particularly during downturns. The other options overstate what Expected Loss covers or misstate when buffers matter.

questionBank.q: A bank discovers that inventory pledged as collateral for a financing facility actually belongs to a third party, not the borrower. Which listed risk of Inventory Financing does this illustrate?
opts: Risk that stocks may become obsolete
Risk of financing inventory to which the borrower has no legal title
Risk that the market price can fall below book value
Risk of losing goods due to fraud or robbery
questionBank.ans: Risk of financing inventory to which the borrower has no legal title
questionBank.exp: This matches the listed risk of financing inventory to which the borrower has no legal title. The other options describe different listed risks — obsolescence, price decline, and loss through fraud or robbery.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a risk specific to Receivable Financing?
opts: Risk that the LPO has expired before delivery of goods
Risk that the bank may finance spurious receivables not accounted for in the borrower's books
Risk of overutilization beyond the approved limit
Risk that a counterparty defaults on a trade payment obligation
questionBank.ans: Risk that the bank may finance spurious receivables not accounted for in the borrower's books
questionBank.exp: Financing spurious receivables not accounted for in the borrower's books is a listed risk specific to Receivable Financing. The other options describe risks specific to LPO Finance, Overdraft Facilities, and Trade Finance respectively.

questionBank.q: Which mitigant for Receivable Financing involves getting the debtor to agree to assign the debt directly to the bank?
opts: Physical inspection of pledged goods
Domiciliation of payment
Establishing validity of the LPO
Collateralization of underlying goods
questionBank.ans: Domiciliation of payment
questionBank.exp: Getting the debtor to agree to assign the debt to the bank is domiciliation of payment, a listed mitigant for Receivable Financing. The other options describe mitigants for Inventory Financing, LPO Finance, and Trade Finance respectively.

questionBank.q: One credit product's specific risk is that the underlying purchase order expires before delivery of goods. A separate product's specific risk is that an exporter or importer defaults on a payment obligation. Which two credit products does this respectively describe?
opts: Trade Finance, then LPO Finance
LPO Finance, then Trade Finance
Inventory Financing, then LPO Finance
LPO Finance, then Inventory Financing
questionBank.ans: LPO Finance, then Trade Finance
questionBank.exp: An expiring purchase order is a listed risk of LPO Finance; exporter/importer default is Counterparty Risk under Trade Finance. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute Inventory Financing.

questionBank.q: A bank discovers that part of a customer's overdraft facility has been quietly used to fund a long-term asset purchase, rather than short-term working capital needs. Which listed Overdraft risk does this illustrate, and what mitigant does the material suggest?
opts: Overutilization Risk, mitigated by clearer terms and conditions on the limit
Hardcore borrowing, mitigated by restructuring the hardcore portion into a Term Loan
Counterparty Risk, mitigated by structured trade finance solutions
Overutilization Risk, mitigated by physical inspection of pledged goods
questionBank.ans: Hardcore borrowing, mitigated by restructuring the hardcore portion into a Term Loan
questionBank.exp: An overdraft diverted to finance a long-term need is Hardcore borrowing, which the material suggests mitigating by restructuring the hardcore portion into a Term Loan (a Cash Flow Lending product). The other options misidentify the risk or attach a mismatched mitigant.

questionBank.q: One credit product's specific risks include financing inventory to which the borrower has no legal title, mitigated by verifying ownership. A separate product's specific risks include financing spurious receivables not recorded in the borrower's books, mitigated by confirming their genuineness. Which two credit products does this respectively describe?
opts: Receivable Financing, then Inventory Financing
Inventory Financing, then Receivable Financing
LPO Finance, then Inventory Financing
Inventory Financing, then LPO Finance
questionBank.ans: Inventory Financing, then Receivable Financing
questionBank.exp: No-legal-title risk mitigated by verifying ownership belongs to Inventory Financing; spurious-receivables risk mitigated by confirming genuineness belongs to Receivable Financing. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute LPO Finance.

questionBank.q: To mitigate Trade Finance risk, a bank structures a transaction using a letter of credit and also collateralizes the transaction using the underlying goods being traded. What type of risk is this combination primarily aimed at mitigating?
opts: Overutilization Risk
Counterparty Risk
Risk of financing an unissued LPO
Risk of stock obsolescence
questionBank.ans: Counterparty Risk
questionBank.exp: Letters of credit and collateralization of underlying goods are listed mitigants specifically for Trade Finance's Counterparty Risk. The other options name risks specific to different credit products.

questionBank.q: Which credit risk management method uses statistical models and algorithms to assign credit scores based on quantitative and qualitative factors, standardizing risk assessment across applicants?
opts: Risk-Based Pricing
Credit Scoring Models
Credit Risk Transfer
Portfolio Diversification
questionBank.ans: Credit Scoring Models
questionBank.exp: Using statistical models to assign standardized credit scores is Credit Scoring Models. The other methods involve adjusting pricing by risk, transferring risk to third parties, and spreading exposure respectively.

questionBank.q: One credit risk management method uses statistical models to assign a standardized score to each borrower. A separate method then uses that risk assessment to adjust the interest rate and terms actually offered to the borrower. Which two methods does this respectively describe?
opts: Risk-Based Pricing, then Credit Scoring Models
Credit Scoring Models, then Risk-Based Pricing
Credit Scoring Models, then Credit Risk Transfer
Early Warning Systems, then Risk-Based Pricing
questionBank.ans: Credit Scoring Models, then Risk-Based Pricing
questionBank.exp: Assigning a standardized score is Credit Scoring Models; using that assessment to adjust pricing and terms is Risk-Based Pricing. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute an unrelated method.

questionBank.q: How is a Loan defined in the material?
opts: An asset pledged by a borrower to reduce a bank's exposure
Money given on condition it is repaid later
A document confirming a borrower's creditworthiness
A fee charged by a bank for processing a credit application
questionBank.ans: Money given on condition it is repaid later
questionBank.exp: A Loan is money given to somebody on the condition that it will be paid back later, admitting of all kinds of bankers' advances by whatever name called. The other options describe collateral, documentation, or fees instead.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed among the Typical Loan Documentation?
opts: Customer's Tax Clearance Certificate
Board Resolution
Marketing Brochure
Bank's Annual Report
questionBank.ans: Board Resolution
questionBank.exp: Board Resolution is one of the six items of Typical Loan Documentation, alongside Offer Letter, Loan Agreements, Security Documentation, Conditions & Covenants, and Guarantees/Indemnities. The other options are not listed loan documentation.

questionBank.q: How is Documentation defined in the material?
opts: Only signed agreements between a lender and a borrower
Reference documents collected as evidence, or providing written information
Only documents that have been registered with a regulatory authority
Only documents prepared after a facility has been fully repaid
questionBank.ans: Reference documents collected as evidence, or providing written information
questionBank.exp: Documentation is defined as evidential or reference documents collected as evidence or reference material, or the process of providing written information about something. The other options narrow this definition to something not stated.

questionBank.q: A dispute arises between a bank and a borrower over what specifically constitutes default under their facility. Which purpose of documentation is most directly relevant to resolving this dispute?
opts: To confirm the relationship between the parties
To determine what constitutes default on the part of any of the parties
To identify any third party to the relationship
To confirm the responsibilities of the relationship
questionBank.ans: To determine what constitutes default on the part of any of the parties
questionBank.exp: Determining what constitutes default on the part of any party is specifically listed among the reasons documentation is important. The other options describe related but distinct purposes not directly aimed at defining default.

questionBank.q: How do the definitions of 'Loan' and 'Lending' respectively differ in what each describes?
opts: Both describe the same act of temporarily transferring money
'Loan' is the money given; 'Lending' is letting something be used temporarily
'Loan' describes the act of letting somebody use something temporarily; 'Lending' describes the money given on condition of repayment
'Loan' and 'Lending' both refer only to the documentation process
questionBank.ans: 'Loan' is the money given; 'Lending' is letting something be used temporarily
questionBank.exp: 'Loan' is the money given on condition it is repaid; 'Lending' is the act of letting somebody use something temporarily subject to its being returned. The other options reverse or misstate this distinction.

questionBank.q: Before a facility can be drawn down, the bank sets out specific conditions the borrower must satisfy, all clearly stated within a single document issued at approval. Which typical loan document is this?
opts: Loan Agreement
Offer Letter
Board Resolution
Security Documentation
questionBank.ans: Offer Letter
questionBank.exp: The Offer Letter specifies the conditions that should be met precedent to drawdown of the facility. The other documents serve different purposes — detailing the full agreement, authorizing signatories, or securing collateral.

questionBank.q: How do the Offer Letter and the Loan Agreement respectively differ in what they are described as specifying?
opts: Both documents specify only the facility amount and nothing else
The Offer Letter sets conditions precedent; the Loan Agreement details full obligations
The Offer Letter details the full obligations of each party; the Loan Agreement specifies only conditions precedent to drawdown
Only the Loan Agreement is used for facilities of any tenor, while the Offer Letter is used solely for short-term facilities
questionBank.ans: The Offer Letter sets conditions precedent; the Loan Agreement details full obligations
questionBank.exp: The Offer Letter states the terms of the offer and conditions precedent to drawdown; the Loan Agreement is the fuller written agreement detailing obligations, rights, and responsibilities of each party. The other options reverse or misstate their respective roles.

questionBank.q: A sole proprietor applies for a facility and is not asked to submit a Board Resolution as part of the loan documentation. Is this consistent with the material?
opts: No, every borrower type must submit a Board Resolution
Yes, since Sole Proprietorships do not have Board Resolutions
No, only Multinational Corporations are exempt from this requirement
Yes, but only if the facility is below a certain amount
questionBank.ans: Yes, since Sole Proprietorships do not have Board Resolutions
questionBank.exp: Board Resolutions are only signed and prepared by Corporations and Partnerships; Sole Proprietorships do not have Board Resolutions. The other options misstate which obligor types this requirement applies to.

questionBank.q: Who is a Board Resolution usually required to be signed by, according to the material?
opts: Any single employee of the company
Two directors, or a director and the secretary
The borrower's external auditor alone
The bank's relationship manager alone
questionBank.ans: Two directors, or a director and the secretary
questionBank.exp: A Board Resolution is usually signed by two directors, or a director and the company secretary, and these must be the most recent directors listed on the current corporate filings. The other options name parties not identified as the required signatories.

questionBank.q: What does the material say about why banks approve loans, in relation to collateral?
opts: Banks approve loans simply because there is adequate collateral
No, banks lend on facilities perceived to be self-liquidating
Banks require collateral for every facility regardless of the borrower's cash flow
Banks never consider collateral when approving a facility
questionBank.ans: No, banks lend on facilities perceived to be self-liquidating
questionBank.exp: Banks typically make loans that are perceived to be self-liquidating, and do not approve loans simply because adequate collateral is present. The other options overstate or deny the role of collateral entirely.

questionBank.q: A borrower pledges an asset that is expected to generate ongoing rental income, which can be redirected to the lender to help repay part or all of an outstanding facility if the borrower defaults. Does this asset fit the material's definition of collateral?
opts: No, only physical property with no income stream can serve as collateral
Yes, since it is an asset producing future cash flow transferable on default
No, since collateral must always be cash or a cash equivalent
Yes, but only if the asset is located outside the country
questionBank.ans: Yes, since it is an asset producing future cash flow transferable on default
questionBank.exp: Collateral is any asset that produces future cash flow directly or indirectly, which can be transferred to a lender for repayment of part or all of an outstanding debt upon default. The other options narrow this definition beyond what the material states.

questionBank.q: How does a benefit of collateral to the bank differ from a benefit of collateral to the customer, based on the material's comparison?
opts: Both lists describe identical benefits to both parties
A bank benefit is enhancing the probability of repayment; a customer benefit is reducing the cost of credit
A bank benefit is reducing the cost of credit; a customer benefit is enhancing the probability of repayment
Neither party is described as benefiting from collateral
questionBank.ans: A bank benefit is enhancing the probability of repayment; a customer benefit is reducing the cost of credit
questionBank.exp: Enhancing the probability of repayment is listed as a benefit to the bank; reducing the cost of credit is listed as a benefit to the customer. The other options reverse or deny this distinction.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a feature of acceptable collateral?
opts: High maintenance cost
Stability of value
Difficulty of verification of title
Ease of pilferage
questionBank.ans: Stability of value
questionBank.exp: Stability of value is a listed feature of acceptable collateral, alongside ease of transfer, low maintenance cost, ease of verification of title, marketability, and not being easily pilfered. The other options describe the opposite of acceptable features.

questionBank.q: An established manufacturer decides to enter an entirely new line of business it has no prior experience in. Based on the material's guidance on When to Take Collateral, should the bank consider requiring security for this facility?
opts: No, an established firm's track record makes security unnecessary regardless of the new venture
Yes, security is desirable for an old firm entering a new business line
No, since When to Take Collateral only applies to relatively new organizations
Yes, but only if the firm is also making losses
questionBank.ans: Yes, security is desirable for an old firm entering a new business line
questionBank.exp: Security is desirable where an organization is relatively new, or an old firm is going into a new line of business. The other options misstate the guidance or add an unstated condition.

questionBank.q: According to the material's guidance on When to Take Collateral, what is usually required of a company that is making losses?
opts: It is automatically exempt from posting collateral
It will usually have to post collateral
It must be referred to another lender
It must convert to a different obligor type
questionBank.ans: It will usually have to post collateral
questionBank.exp: A company that is making losses will usually have to post collateral. The other options describe outcomes not supported by the material.

questionBank.q: According to the material, why is there always a collateral coverage margin, with collateral valued higher than the amount lent?
opts: Because regulators require collateral to always be worth exactly double the loan amount
Collateral may fall in value, unserviced interest accrues, and sale costs money
Because the borrower's credit score determines the exact margin required in all cases
Because collateral coverage is only relevant for facilities longer than five years
questionBank.ans: Collateral may fall in value, unserviced interest accrues, and sale costs money
questionBank.exp: The margin exists because the asset may fall in value, the loan continues to attract interest if not serviced, and the bank incurs costs — possibly selling at an unfavourable price — if it must sell the asset. The other options invent requirements not stated in the material.

questionBank.q: One piece of collateral is a parcel of land and the building on it. A separate piece of collateral is a company's book debt owed to it by its customers. Which two collateral type categories does this respectively describe?
opts: Goods, then Intangibles
Immovable Collateral, then Intangibles
Intangibles, then Immovable Collateral
Immovable Collateral, then Goods
questionBank.ans: Immovable Collateral, then Intangibles
questionBank.exp: Land and buildings fall under Immovable Collateral; book debt falls under Intangibles. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute the Goods category instead.

questionBank.q: A bank officer notices that the market price of a piece of collateral has been rising unusually fast over a short period. Based on the material's Principles of Collateral Evaluation, what should this rapid rise prompt the officer to consider?
opts: Nothing, since a rising price is always straightforwardly positive for collateral coverage
That a price bubble may be developing, and the price should be watched carefully
That the collateral should immediately be revalued upward and accepted without further scrutiny
That the asset should automatically be reclassified as a different collateral type
questionBank.ans: That a price bubble may be developing, and the price should be watched carefully
questionBank.exp: The material specifically advises watching the market price if it is rising fast, since a price bubble may be developing. The other options treat the rapid rise as unambiguously positive or invent an unrelated response.

questionBank.q: What does the material say a lender should do regarding the value of collateral once it has been taken?
opts: Assume its value remains fixed for the life of the facility
Review its value regularly and cover any shortfall
Review its value only once, at the point the facility is disbursed
Rely entirely on the borrower's own valuation without independent verification
questionBank.ans: Review its value regularly and cover any shortfall
questionBank.exp: A regular review of collateral value should be performed, with any shortfall compared to the outstanding facility amount covered. The other options describe a static or unverified approach the material does not support.

questionBank.q: A bank takes a specific security over a borrower's key asset, placing itself in a superior position relative to other creditors of that borrower. How does the material describe the position of other lenders who hold no such specific security, relative to this bank?
opts: They rank equally with the bank in every respect
To the senior lender, all junior lenders are effectively equity
They automatically take priority over the bank regardless of its specific security
Their claims are extinguished entirely once the bank takes specific security
questionBank.ans: To the senior lender, all junior lenders are effectively equity
questionBank.exp: The material states that to the senior lender holding specific security, all junior lenders are effectively equity. The other options misstate the relative position this creates.

questionBank.q: A bank creates a charge over a company's assets but fails to register it at the Corporate Affairs Commission within 90 days of creation. Based on the material's Dangers of Not Perfecting, what is the consequence?
opts: The charge remains fully valid indefinitely without any registration
The charge becomes void, and the bank will need a court order to revive it
The charge automatically converts into a Legal Mortgage
The charge is suspended for 90 additional days before taking effect
questionBank.ans: The charge becomes void, and the bank will need a court order to revive it
questionBank.exp: A charge not registered at the CAC within 90 days of creation is void, and the bank will need a court order after 90 days to revive it. The other options misstate the consequence of late registration.

questionBank.q: A borrower defaults on a facility before the bank has completed perfection of its security documents. Based on the material's Dangers of Not Perfecting, what position does the bank find itself in?
opts: The position of a fully secured creditor, as if perfection had already occurred
The position of an unsecured creditor
The position of a preferential creditor ahead of all other claims
The position of a guarantor rather than a lender
questionBank.ans: The position of an unsecured creditor
questionBank.exp: Should there be default before perfection, the bank will be in the position of an unsecured creditor. The other options overstate the bank's protection in this situation.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed among the Common Types of Securities for Bank Loans?
opts: Board Resolution
Debentures
Offer Letter
Personal Financial Statement
questionBank.ans: Debentures
questionBank.exp: Debentures is one of the ten listed Common Types of Securities, alongside Mortgages, Lien, Guarantees and indemnities, Negative pledge, Right of set-off, Letter of comfort, Charge over credit balance, Domiciliation of payment, and Letter of hypothecation. The other options are loan documentation, not security types.

questionBank.q: A borrower takes formal steps to convey legal interest in a property to the bank by registering an instrument of transfer in the office designated for it, and no court consent is needed to sell the property on default. Which type of mortgage is this?
opts: Equitable Mortgage
Legal Mortgage
Floating Charge Debenture
Fixed Charge Debenture
questionBank.ans: Legal Mortgage
questionBank.exp: Registering an instrument of transfer to convey legal interest, with no court consent needed to sell, describes a Legal Mortgage. The other options describe a weaker security requiring court cooperation or unrelated debenture types.

questionBank.q: A borrower simply deposits property title documents with the bank as security, without registering any formal instrument of transfer, and on default the bank would need the borrower's cooperation or a court order to sell. Which type of mortgage is this?
opts: Legal Mortgage
Equitable Mortgage
All Asset Debenture
Mortgage Debenture
questionBank.ans: Equitable Mortgage
questionBank.exp: Merely depositing title documents, with cooperation or a court order needed to sell on default, describes an Equitable Mortgage. The other options describe the stronger Legal Mortgage or unrelated debenture types.

questionBank.q: How do Legal Mortgages and Equitable Mortgages respectively differ in what is required to sell the property on default?
opts: Both require a court order before the property can be sold
A Legal Mortgage needs no court order; an Equitable Mortgage may need one
A Legal Mortgage requires a court order; an Equitable Mortgage does not require one
Neither requires anything further before sale, as both are equally strong
questionBank.ans: A Legal Mortgage needs no court order; an Equitable Mortgage may need one
questionBank.exp: A Legal Mortgage is a good title that does not require court consent to sell; an Equitable Mortgage is weaker and requires either the mortgagor's cooperation or a court order to sell. The other options reverse or deny this distinction.

questionBank.q: What is a Certificate of Occupancy described as evidence of?
opts: A registered power of attorney over a property
Title to land sold by the government (State or Federal)
A tripartite domiciliation agreement
A company's floating charge over its stock-in-trade
questionBank.ans: Title to land sold by the government (State or Federal)
questionBank.exp: A Certificate of Occupancy is evidence of title to land sold by the government, whether State or Federal. The other options describe different land title documents or unrelated security concepts.

questionBank.q: A parcel of land is transferred from a deceased owner to their heirs, with no last will and testament in place. Which land title document is used in this transfer?
opts: A registered deed of assignment
Letters of administration
A right of occupancy
A power of attorney
questionBank.ans: Letters of administration
questionBank.exp: Letters of administration are used when land is transferred from one person to another by reason of death, where there is no last will and testament. The other options describe transfers between living parties or a different form of title.

questionBank.q: How does CAMA 1990 (S650(1)) define a debenture?
opts: A verbal agreement between a company and its bank regarding repayment
A written acknowledgement of company indebtedness and its terms
A certificate confirming a company has no outstanding liabilities
A document used exclusively to transfer land title
questionBank.ans: A written acknowledgement of company indebtedness and its terms
questionBank.exp: CAMA 1990 defines a debenture as a written acknowledgement of indebtedness by the company, setting the terms and conditions of indebtedness, including debenture stock, bonds, and other securities whether or not constituting a charge on the company's assets. The other options misstate this definition.

questionBank.q: A charge is created over a company's specifically listed immovable assets, excluding its landed property, and those assets cannot be sold without the bank's consent. Which type of debenture is this?
opts: Floating Charge Debenture
Fixed Charge Debenture
All Asset Debenture
Pari-Passu Debenture
questionBank.ans: Fixed Charge Debenture
questionBank.exp: A charge on specifically listed immovable assets, excluding land, requiring bank consent to sell, is a Fixed Charge Debenture. The other options describe a charge on current assets, a charge over all assets, or equal-ranking charges respectively.

questionBank.q: A charge is created over a company's current assets and stock-in-trade, and prior to default, those assets can be sold without the bank's consent being sought or obtained. Which type of debenture is this?
opts: Fixed Charge Debenture
Floating Charge Debenture
Mortgage Debenture
All Asset Debenture
questionBank.ans: Floating Charge Debenture
questionBank.exp: A charge on current assets or stock-in-trade, sellable without consent prior to default, is a Floating Charge Debenture. The other options describe a charge on specific immovable assets, a charge including Legal Mortgage, or a charge over all assets respectively.

questionBank.q: How do the All Asset Debenture and the Mortgage Debenture respectively differ in their treatment of land?
opts: Both automatically include land within their charge
All Asset excludes land; Mortgage Debenture includes a Legal Mortgage
The All Asset Debenture is a charge including Legal Mortgage over land; the Mortgage Debenture excludes land entirely
Neither debenture type has any relationship to land
questionBank.ans: All Asset excludes land; Mortgage Debenture includes a Legal Mortgage
questionBank.exp: The All Asset Debenture is a charge over all assets excluding land, which must be specifically mortgaged; the Mortgage Debenture is a charge over fixed and floating assets including a Legal Mortgage. The other options reverse or deny this distinction.

questionBank.q: A borrower makes a physical transfer of a valuable item to the lender as security, but retains legal title to the item throughout, with the lender holding only possession until the loan is repaid. Which type of security is this?
opts: A Debenture
A Pledge
A Negative Pledge
A Letter of Hypothecation
questionBank.ans: A Pledge
questionBank.exp: A Pledge is created when the borrower makes a physical or constructive transfer of property to the lender as security, with the lender keeping possession while the borrower keeps legal title. The other options describe different security types with different possession/title arrangements.

questionBank.q: How do a Guarantee and an Indemnity respectively differ in the position of the third party providing them?
opts: Both make the third party a secondary obligor with indirect exposure
A Guarantee is secondary/indirect; an Indemnity is primary/direct
In a Guarantee, the third party is a primary obligor with direct exposure; in an Indemnity, the third party is a secondary obligor with indirect exposure
Both make the third party a primary obligor with direct exposure
questionBank.ans: A Guarantee is secondary/indirect; an Indemnity is primary/direct
questionBank.exp: A guarantor is a secondary obligor with indirect exposure, liable only if the borrower fails to pay; an indemnifier is a primary obligor with direct exposure, undertaking to repay from inception. The other options reverse or deny this distinction.

questionBank.q: When obtaining a third-party guarantee or indemnity from an individual, what must the bank also obtain, and why?
opts: A copy of the guarantor's school certificates, to confirm their educational background
A sworn statement of net worth, since a false statement is perjury
A letter from the guarantor's employer confirming their job title only
Nothing further, since the guarantee or indemnity alone is always sufficient
questionBank.ans: A sworn statement of net worth, since a false statement is perjury
questionBank.exp: The bank must obtain a statement of net worth signed as an affidavit, because a false statement made under oath constitutes perjury, which is punishable by imprisonment. The other options name documents not required for this purpose or deny the requirement entirely.

questionBank.q: A bank obtains a personal guarantee from an individual but does not require a statement of net worth signed as an affidavit. Based on the material's stated practice, is this adequate?
opts: Yes, since a guarantee alone is always sufficient regardless of any net worth statement
No, a sworn net worth statement is also required for third-party guarantees
Yes, but only because affidavits are optional formalities with no real legal weight
No, but only if the guarantor is a corporate entity rather than an individual
questionBank.ans: No, a sworn net worth statement is also required for third-party guarantees
questionBank.exp: The material states that a statement of net worth signed as an affidavit must also be obtained when taking a third-party guarantee or indemnity from an individual, precisely because of the legal weight a sworn statement carries. The other options dismiss this requirement or misstate when it applies.

questionBank.q: A reputable borrower commits not to pledge any of its assets to a third party without the knowledge of its existing lender, but this commitment does not grant the existing lender any actual right over the borrower's assets. Which type of security is this?
opts: Right of Set-off
Negative Pledge
Letter of Hypothecation
Lien on Account
questionBank.ans: Negative Pledge
questionBank.exp: A Negative Pledge is a commitment by a reputable borrower not to encumber its assets in favour of a third party without the existing lender's knowledge, and it does not confer rights on any asset — merely restricting the borrower's ability to give security to others. The other options describe securities that do involve a direct claim over specific assets or balances.

questionBank.q: A borrower holds two accounts with the same bank. When the borrower defaults on one account, the bank uses the credit balance in the other account to offset the outstanding debit. Which type of security is this?
opts: Negative Pledge
Right of Set-off
Letter of Comfort
Domiciliation of Payment
questionBank.ans: Right of Set-off
questionBank.exp: Using the credit balance in one account to offset a debit balance in another account of the same customer is Right of Set-off. The other options describe a restriction on encumbering assets, a quasi-security letter, or a tripartite payment arrangement respectively.

questionBank.q: How do a Negative Pledge and a Right of Set-off respectively differ in what they give the lender a claim over?
opts: Both give the lender a direct claim over the borrower's specific assets
A Negative Pledge confers no asset rights; a Right of Set-off uses other account balances
A Negative Pledge gives the lender use of credit balances in other accounts; a Right of Set-off confers no rights over any asset
Neither security gives the lender any claim or restriction of any kind
questionBank.ans: A Negative Pledge confers no asset rights; a Right of Set-off uses other account balances
questionBank.exp: A Negative Pledge confers no rights on any asset, merely restricting the borrower's ability to grant security to others; a Right of Set-off allows the lender to use credit balances in the borrower's other accounts to offset a debit. The other options reverse or deny this distinction.

questionBank.q: Why is it advised that a Letter of Comfort be accompanied by a tangible security as backup?
opts: Because a Letter of Comfort is legally identical to a Legal Mortgage
It is a quasi-security with no attached liability
Because a Letter of Comfort automatically becomes void after 90 days
Because a Letter of Comfort can only be issued by a government agency
questionBank.ans: It is a quasi-security with no attached liability
questionBank.exp: A Letter of Comfort is a quasi-security because no liability is attached to it — it merely states the obligor is fit and proper as a prospective borrower — so a tangible security is advised as backup. The other options misstate its nature or invent unrelated claims.

questionBank.q: A borrower expressly requests that a third party who owes them money — such as an employer paying a salary — pay those amounts directly to the lending bank instead, under a tripartite arrangement among the borrower, the third party, and the bank. Which type of security is this?
opts: Letter of Hypothecation
Domiciliation of Payment
Right of Set-off
Negative Pledge
questionBank.ans: Domiciliation of Payment
questionBank.exp: A tripartite agreement where a third party is directed to pay amounts due to the borrower directly to the bank is Domiciliation of Payment, commonly used for short-term retail facilities or against an employee's salary. The other options describe different security arrangements.

questionBank.q: One security operates where it is impracticable to give the bank possession of goods or their document of title. A separate security lets a customer charge as security their credit balance in a fixed, current, savings, or domiciliary account. Which two securities does this respectively describe?
opts: Lien on Account, then Letter of Hypothecation
Letter of Hypothecation, then Lien on Account
Letter of Hypothecation, then Right of Set-off
Negative Pledge, then Lien on Account
questionBank.ans: Letter of Hypothecation, then Lien on Account
questionBank.exp: A Letter of Hypothecation applies where possession of goods can't practicably be given to the bank; a Lien on Account lets a customer charge a credit balance across various account types. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute unrelated securities.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a Major Documentation Error/Pitfall?
opts: Requiring too much insurance cover on secured assets
Acceptance of forged or cloned documentation
Reviewing collateral value too frequently
Registering a charge too early
questionBank.ans: Acceptance of forged or cloned documentation
questionBank.exp: Acceptance of forged or cloned documentation is listed among the Major Documentation Errors/Pitfalls, alongside failure to perfect security and inadequate insurance cover. The other options describe practices the material does not list as pitfalls.

questionBank.q: A bank takes insurance-covered collateral on a facility but never formally lists itself as the loss payee on the policy. Which Major Documentation Error/Pitfall does this illustrate?
opts: Improperly executed loan agreements
Failure to ensure listing of the bank as 'loss payee'
Absence of properly executed security documents
Poor financial statements revealing little about project viability
questionBank.ans: Failure to ensure listing of the bank as 'loss payee'
questionBank.exp: This scenario directly matches the listed pitfall of failing to ensure the bank is listed as 'loss payee.' The other options describe different listed pitfalls not illustrated by this scenario.

questionBank.q: A bank accepts a Letter of Comfort as the sole form of security for a facility, with no tangible security backing it. Based on the material's description of a Letter of Comfort, is this adequate practice?
opts: Yes, since a Letter of Comfort carries the same legal liability as a Guarantee
No, it carries no liability and should be backed by tangible security
Yes, since Letters of Comfort are only ever issued by government agencies with full backing
No, but only because Letters of Comfort are never accepted by banks under any circumstances
questionBank.ans: No, it carries no liability and should be backed by tangible security
questionBank.exp: Because no liability is attached to a Letter of Comfort, the material advises it be accompanied by tangible security as backup — relying on it alone leaves the bank without real recourse. The other options overstate its legal weight or misstate whether it is ever accepted.

questionBank.q: A bank secures a facility with a charge over a customer's fixed deposit balance held at the same bank, rather than over any physical or intangible business asset. Which type of security does this most directly represent?
opts: Letter of Hypothecation
Charge over credit balance
Negative Pledge
Floating Charge Debenture
questionBank.ans: Charge over credit balance
questionBank.exp: A charge over a customer's own credit balance, such as a fixed deposit, is Charge over credit balance, one of the ten listed Common Types of Securities. The other options describe securities over goods, a restrictive covenant not conferring asset rights, or a charge over stock-in-trade respectively.

questionBank.q: Where does the loan monitoring process begin, according to the material?
opts: With the Relationship Team, immediately after facility disbursement
With the Credit Control Desk before disbursement
With the Legal Department, roughly one year after disbursement
With the Loan Recovery Department, once a facility is classified
questionBank.ans: With the Credit Control Desk before disbursement
questionBank.exp: The loan monitoring process starts with the Credit Control Desk before disbursement by the Credit Administration Unit. The other options misplace where the process begins.

questionBank.q: Before allowing a credit to proceed, an officer checks it against the bank's target market definition, risk acceptance criteria, approval limits, and minimum risk-adjusted return. Which function within the loan monitoring process is being carried out?
opts: The Loan Recovery Department's post-default review of the account
The Credit Control Desk's review against the Credit Policy Guide
The bank's Realization of Security on pledged collateral
The branch's Portfolio-level Turnover Reporting exercise
questionBank.ans: The Credit Control Desk's review against the Credit Policy Guide
questionBank.exp: Checking a credit against the Credit Policy Guide's stipulations — target market, risk acceptance criteria, approval limits, and minimum risk-adjusted return — is the Credit Control Desk's role. The other options describe later-stage or unrelated functions.

questionBank.q: Which department is specifically responsible for overseeing completeness of documentation and security, according to the material?
opts: The Marketing Department
The Legal Department
The Human Resources Department
The External Audit Department
questionBank.ans: The Legal Department
questionBank.exp: Emphasis on completeness of documentation and security is specifically overseen by the Legal Department. The other departments are not assigned this role in the material.

questionBank.q: A relationship officer attends a customer's child's naming ceremony and, separately, visits the customer's factory premises to hold discussions. Which aspect of the loan monitoring process do both activities represent?
opts: Portfolio-level reporting
Forms of observation used in monitoring
Realization of security
The Credit Control Desk's pre-disbursement review
questionBank.ans: Forms of observation used in monitoring
questionBank.exp: Attending social events and visiting the customer's premises are both listed as forms of observation used in monitoring, alongside reviewing the account and reading newspapers and magazines. The other options describe different, unrelated stages of credit management.

questionBank.q: An officer records in the credit file the explanation a customer gave for a cheque that was drawn against insufficient funds. What does the material say should be done with observations and explanations like this?
opts: They should be discarded once the account returns to normal
They should be noted in the credit file
They should only be shared with the customer's competitors
They are irrelevant to the risk management department
questionBank.ans: They should be noted in the credit file
questionBank.exp: The material specifically states that such observations and explanations should be noted in the credit file, and made available to the risk management department. The other options contradict this practice.

questionBank.q: What is the minimum frequency of periodic reporting on credit facilities described in the material?
opts: At least a weekly report showing only the facilities currently in arrears
A monthly report on all facilities, balances, limits, and expiry dates
At least an annual report showing only the bank's total loan book size
At least a quarterly report showing only newly approved facilities
questionBank.ans: A monthly report on all facilities, balances, limits, and expiry dates
questionBank.exp: At least a monthly report is required, showing all credit facilities, their balances, agreed limits, and expiry dates. The other options misstate the frequency or narrow what the report should cover.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as content included in Risk Management's periodic reports?
opts: The borrower's personal astrological sign
Classification and provision made
The borrower's preferred holiday destination
The number of branches the borrower's competitors operate
questionBank.ans: Classification and provision made
questionBank.exp: Classification and provision made are listed among the contents of Risk Management's periodic reports, alongside limit, amount borrowed, current balance, and collateral details. The other options are not listed report contents.

questionBank.q: A branch holds a meeting specifically to review all its credit facilities and agree on actions needed to secure repayment of its non-performing facilities. What does the material say this kind of activity represents?
opts: An optional formality with no real bearing on credit management
Reporting as communication, a key aspect of credit management
A substitute for the Credit Control Desk's pre-disbursement review
A step required only once a facility has already been charged off
questionBank.ans: Reporting as communication, a key aspect of credit management
questionBank.exp: The material describes such branch review meetings as part of reporting, which is about communication and a key aspect of credit management. The other options dismiss its importance or misplace it in the process.

questionBank.q: One portfolio-level report lets a Loan Officer direct the Clearing Department to return a cheque unpaid due to an unfunded account. A separate report shows which credits have been booked each day, allowing booking limit breaches to be sanctioned. Which two portfolio-level reports does this respectively describe?
opts: Deal Booked Daily, then Unfunded Accounts for Clearing Cheques
Unfunded Accounts for Clearing Cheques, then Deal Booked Daily
Future Maturities Report, then Turnover Report
Unfunded Accounts for Clearing Cheques, then Future Maturities Report
questionBank.ans: Unfunded Accounts for Clearing Cheques, then Deal Booked Daily
questionBank.exp: Directing the return of an unpaid cheque due to an unfunded account is the Unfunded Accounts for Clearing Cheques report; showing daily bookings to sanction limit breaches is the Deal Booked Daily report. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute unrelated reports.

questionBank.q: A Loan Officer reviewing portfolio-level reports notices a facility flagged as having been disbursed before its conditions precedent were fully met. What does this flag most directly call for?
opts: No action, since the facility has already been disbursed and cannot be reviewed further
Prompt follow-up, since this report exists specifically to surface this kind of gap for attention
Automatic charge-off of the facility, without further investigation
Immediate reporting to the Central Bank of Nigeria, bypassing internal review
questionBank.ans: Prompt follow-up, since this report exists specifically to surface this kind of gap for attention
questionBank.exp: This report exists specifically to surface facilities disbursed before conditions precedent were met, so it should prompt follow-up rather than being ignored. The other options either dismiss the flag or escalate disproportionately without internal review first.

questionBank.q: How are Early Warning Signals defined in the material?
opts: A formal legal notice sent only after a loan has already defaulted
Certain observable traits exhibited by a loan that is about to go bad
A mandatory annual audit of the bank's entire loan portfolio
A rating assigned by an external credit bureau
questionBank.ans: Certain observable traits exhibited by a loan that is about to go bad
questionBank.exp: Early warning signals are defined as certain observable traits exhibited by a loan that is about to go bad, requiring a loan officer's discernment to identify, follow up, and escalate. The other options describe different, unrelated concepts.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as one of the nine categories of Early Warning Signals?
opts: Regulatory Signals
Economic Signals
Currency Signals
Reputational Signals
questionBank.ans: Economic Signals
questionBank.exp: Economic Signals is one of the nine listed categories, alongside Account Activity, Management, Managerial, Business, Information, Income Statement, Cash Flow, and Liquidity Concern and Crunch. The other options are not among the nine named categories.

questionBank.q: A customer's account frequently exceeds its approved limit, shows little turnover, and generates a reducing yield to the bank. Which category of Early Warning Signal does this illustrate?
opts: Business Signals
Account Activity Signals
Information Signals
Economic Signals
questionBank.ans: Account Activity Signals
questionBank.exp: Frequent excess over limit, little turnover, and reducing yield on account are all listed under Account Activity Signals. The other categories concern the business's operations, information flow, and the broader economy respectively.

questionBank.q: A business owner begins showing changing personal habits and develops a gambling problem, alongside a growing lack of cooperation with the bank. Which category of Early Warning Signal does this illustrate?
opts: Cash Flow Signals
Management Signals
Income Statement Signals
Account Activity Signals
questionBank.ans: Management Signals
questionBank.exp: Changing personal habits, gambling problems, and lack of cooperation are all listed under Management Signals. The other categories concern cash generation, financial statement trends, and account-level activity respectively.

questionBank.q: One signal is the loss of key product lines, distribution rights, or sources of supply. A separate signal is credit enquiries about the customer being made by other banks. Which two categories of Early Warning Signal does this respectively describe?
opts: Information Signals, then Business Signals
Business Signals, then Information Signals
Business Signals, then Economic Signals
Management Signals, then Information Signals
questionBank.ans: Business Signals, then Information Signals
questionBank.exp: Loss of key product lines, distribution rights, or supply sources is a Business Signal; credit enquiries by other banks is an Information Signal. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute a different category.

questionBank.q: One warning sign is declining sales combined with high fixed costs and a significant decline in margin. A separate warning sign is growing income alongside falling cash generated from operations. Which two categories of Early Warning Signal does this respectively describe?
opts: Cash Flow Signals, then Income Statement & Balance Sheet Signals
Income Statement & Balance Sheet Signals, then Cash Flow Signals
Business Signals, then Economic Signals
Income Statement & Balance Sheet Signals, then Business Signals
questionBank.ans: Income Statement & Balance Sheet Signals, then Cash Flow Signals
questionBank.exp: Declining sales, high fixed costs, and margin decline are Income Statement & Balance Sheet Signals; growing income with falling operating cash flow is a Cash Flow Signal. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute unrelated categories.

questionBank.q: An industry sees a wave of new competitors enter at once, alongside oversupply relative to demand. Which category of Early Warning Signal does this illustrate?
opts: Management Signals
Economic Signals
Account Activity Signals
Information Signals
questionBank.ans: Economic Signals
questionBank.exp: Influx of new entrants and an oversupply factor are both listed under Economic Signals. The other categories concern personal/behavioural traits, account-level activity, and information flow respectively.

questionBank.q: One category of signal concerns account-level symptoms like frequent excess over limit and returned cheques. A separate category concerns broader personal and behavioural traits of the borrower, like changing habits and lack of successor management. Which two categories does this respectively describe?
opts: Management Signals, then Account Activity Signals
Account Activity Signals, then Management Signals
Account Activity Signals, then Business Signals
Cash Flow Signals, then Management Signals
questionBank.ans: Account Activity Signals, then Management Signals
questionBank.exp: Excess over limit and returned cheques are Account Activity Signals; changing habits and lack of successor management are Management Signals. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute a different category.

questionBank.q: A loan officer notices signals spanning several categories at once on one account — reduced account turnover, a key customer lost, and delayed financial statements. What does the material say the officer should do upon identifying such signals?
opts: Wait until the facility is already in arrears before taking any action
Proactively follow up and escalate the situation for timely management intervention
Immediately call in the facility without further investigation
Ignore signals that span more than one category, since each must be assessed separately
questionBank.ans: Proactively follow up and escalate the situation for timely management intervention
questionBank.exp: Early warning signals require a loan officer's discernment to proactively identify, promptly follow up, and escalate for timely management intervention — regardless of how many categories are involved. The other options describe inaction, premature escalation, or an unsupported restriction.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a Management Signal in the material?
opts: Rapidly changing business or industry
Rapidly growing one-man operations
Rising selling, general and administration expenses
Government restrictive policy on the industry
questionBank.ans: Rapidly growing one-man operations
questionBank.exp: Rapidly growing one-man operations is listed under Management Signals. The other options are listed under Business, Income Statement, and Economic Signals respectively.

questionBank.q: One concept describes a bank making a full demand for repayment of the entire outstanding balance after default persists. A separate concept describes the bank selling deposited security because the customer is unable to pay. Which two concepts does this respectively describe?
opts: Realization of Security, then Call In
Call In, then Realization of Security
Work Out, then Charge-Off
Call In, then Charge-Off
questionBank.ans: Call In, then Realization of Security
questionBank.exp: A full demand for repayment after persistent default is a Call In; selling deposited security when the customer cannot pay is Realization of Security. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute Work Out or Charge-Off.

questionBank.q: A struggling customer brings the bank a proposal for how they intend to repay their outstanding loan. The analyst reviews the proposal's viability before it is put to the credit committee for a final decision. Which restructuring/remedial concept is this?
opts: Call In
Work Out
Realization of Security
Foreclosure on Collaterals
questionBank.ans: Work Out
questionBank.exp: A customer-initiated repayment proposal, checked for viability by the analyst before a credit committee decision, is a Work Out. The other options describe a full repayment demand, a sale of security, or a distinct loan recovery method.

questionBank.q: What does REPAYMENT/CHARGE-OFF involve, according to the material?
opts: Automatically forgiving the loan with no committee review required
Writing off the loan, subject to committee approval
Transferring the loan to another bank without the customer's knowledge
Converting the outstanding loan into equity in the business
questionBank.ans: Writing off the loan, subject to committee approval
questionBank.exp: Charge-off means writing off the loan against the bank's profit, with the analyst writing a credit report seeking approval, which the credit committee must grant. The other options misstate the process or invent steps not described.

questionBank.q: A credit committee reviews a proposed charge-off on a defaulted facility and declines to approve it. Based on the material, what happens next?
opts: The loan is automatically written off regardless of the committee's decision
The customer may be further pursued, since a charge-off may be declined
The bank is legally barred from taking any further recovery action
The facility is immediately converted into a Work Out arrangement
questionBank.ans: The customer may be further pursued, since a charge-off may be declined
questionBank.exp: The material states that a charge-off may be declined and the customer further pursued, meaning declining the charge-off does not end recovery efforts. The other options misstate what follows a declined charge-off.

questionBank.q: What do Loan Workout Techniques depend on, according to the material?
opts: The customer's age and gender only
The underlying peculiarities and circumstances of the loan
The bank's total number of branches nationwide
The interest rate prevailing at loan origination only
questionBank.ans: The underlying peculiarities and circumstances of the loan
questionBank.exp: Loan Workout Techniques depend on the underlying peculiarities and circumstances of the loan. The other options name factors not identified as the basis for selecting a technique.

questionBank.q: A bank converts a struggling customer's overdraft facility into a term loan, with a structured repayment schedule replacing the revolving arrangement. Which Loan Workout Technique is this?
opts: Granting a Moratorium
Restructuring
Administrative Effort
Realization of Security
questionBank.ans: Restructuring
questionBank.exp: Converting an overdraft into a term loan is listed as a form of Restructuring. The other options describe deferring payments, write-off/refund/forgiveness measures, or selling pledged security respectively.

questionBank.q: A bank grants a struggling customer a temporary suspension of principal repayment obligations, while interest continues to accrue. Which Loan Workout Technique is this?
opts: Administrative Effort involving write-off or debt forgiveness
Granting of Moratorium on Principal and/or Interest
Restructuring of the facility's fundamental terms
Charge-Off against the bank's own profit
questionBank.ans: Granting of Moratorium on Principal and/or Interest
questionBank.exp: A temporary suspension of principal (and/or interest) repayment is a Moratorium. The other options describe different techniques — changing facility terms, write-off/refund/forgiveness measures, and writing off the loan entirely.

questionBank.q: One workout technique changes a facility's terms, such as converting an overdraft into a term loan or extending its tenor. A separate technique involves write-offs, interest refunds, or debt forgiveness with no change to the facility's terms. Which two techniques does this respectively describe?
opts: Administrative Effort, then Restructuring
Restructuring, then Administrative Effort
Rescheduling, then Moratorium
Restructuring, then Moratorium
questionBank.ans: Restructuring, then Administrative Effort
questionBank.exp: Changing a facility's terms, such as converting an overdraft into a term loan, is Restructuring; write-offs, interest refunds, and debt forgiveness fall under Administrative Effort. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute unrelated techniques.

questionBank.q: Debt Forgiveness is listed as a Loan Workout Technique under Administrative Effort. Referral to External Solicitors for Legal Action is listed as a Loan Recovery Method, cautioned as taking time and resources. Which broader processes do these two concepts respectively belong to?
opts: Loan Recovery, then Loan Workout Techniques
Loan Workout Techniques, then Loan Recovery
Early Warning Signals, then Loan Recovery
Loan Workout Techniques, then Early Warning Signals
questionBank.ans: Loan Workout Techniques, then Loan Recovery
questionBank.exp: Debt Forgiveness under Administrative Effort belongs to Loan Workout Techniques; Referral to External Solicitors belongs to Loan Recovery Methods. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute Early Warning Signals.

questionBank.q: A bank keeps a struggling customer's overdraft facility in place but also amends the repayment schedule so that due dates align more closely with the customer's actual cash flow patterns. Which Loan Workout Technique sub-category is this?
opts: Restructuring
Rescheduling of Repayments
Administrative Effort
Realization of Security
questionBank.ans: Rescheduling of Repayments
questionBank.exp: Amending the repayment schedule to match cash flow patterns is listed under Rescheduling of Repayments. The other options describe changing the facility's fundamental terms, write-off/refund/forgiveness measures, or selling pledged security respectively.

questionBank.q: According to the Loan Recovery Process, what is the Relationship Manager's role once a loan shows signs of default?
opts: To immediately transfer the customer's account to another branch office
Identify default reasons and find ways to recover the loan
To automatically approve a charge-off without any further committee review
To wait for the Central Bank to formally instruct the next recovery steps
questionBank.ans: Identify default reasons and find ways to recover the loan
questionBank.exp: The Relationship Manager must try to identify the reasons for default and find ways to get the loan recovered or regularized. The other options describe actions not assigned to the RM in this role.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as one of the essential measures to prevent a loan from becoming sticky?
opts: Delaying any follow-up until the loan is fully classified
Close monitoring during the validity/repayment period of the loan
Avoiding direct contact with the borrower once default begins
Waiting for the borrower to initiate all communication
questionBank.ans: Close monitoring during the validity/repayment period of the loan
questionBank.exp: Close monitoring during the validity/repayment period of the loan is one of the essential measures listed, alongside gearing up persuasion early, understanding reasons for non-payment, and constant follow-up. The other options describe the opposite of sound practice.

questionBank.q: A bank sends a defaulting customer a formal letter appealing to them to settle their outstanding obligation, without yet resorting to legal action or selling any pledged asset. Which Loan Recovery Method is this?
opts: Foreclosure on Collaterals
Moral Suasion and Appeals
Appointment of a Receiver Manager
Referral to External Solicitors
questionBank.ans: Moral Suasion and Appeals
questionBank.exp: A formal letter of demand appealing to the customer to settle is listed under Moral Suasion and Appeals. The other options describe selling pledged assets, appointing a manager to run or liquidate the company, and pursuing legal action respectively.

questionBank.q: One recovery method is a formal letter appealing to the customer to settle voluntarily, without legal action. A separate method involves selling the assets pledged as security for the facility. Which two Loan Recovery Methods does this respectively describe?
opts: Foreclosure on Collaterals, then Moral Suasion and Appeals
Moral Suasion and Appeals, then Foreclosure on Collaterals
Moral Suasion and Appeals, then Referral to External Solicitors
Reporting to Central Bank, then Foreclosure on Collaterals
questionBank.ans: Moral Suasion and Appeals, then Foreclosure on Collaterals
questionBank.exp: A formal letter appealing to the customer is Moral Suasion and Appeals; selling pledged security is Foreclosure on Collaterals. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute a different recovery method.

questionBank.q: A company has defaulted on a significant facility, and the bank appoints a Receiver Manager. Based on the material, what is the purpose of this appointment?
opts: To provide the company with a temporary moratorium on all repayments
To manage or liquidate the company
To act solely as an intermediary for moral suasion and appeals
To formally waive the bank's claim on the company's assets
questionBank.ans: To manage or liquidate the company
questionBank.exp: Appointment of a Receiver Manager is a listed recovery method used to manage or liquidate the company. The other options describe different, unrelated remedial actions.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a purpose of the Future Maturities Report, one of the portfolio-level reports available to Loan Management Officers?
opts: Showing only facilities that have already been charged off
Showing facilities approaching their maturity date
Showing the bank's total number of branches
Showing only facilities secured by a Legal Mortgage
questionBank.ans: Showing facilities approaching their maturity date
questionBank.exp: The Future Maturities Report is listed among portfolio-level reports, showing facilities approaching their maturity date so they can be monitored ahead of time. The other options describe content not tied to this report.

questionBank.q: A struggling company starts acquiring assets that reflect what management 'wants' rather than what the business actually 'needs,' even as its cash position weakens. Which category of Early Warning Signal does this illustrate?
opts: Business Signals
Cash Flow Signals
Economic Signals
Account Activity Signals
questionBank.ans: Cash Flow Signals
questionBank.exp: Acquiring assets representing 'wants' rather than 'needs' is listed under Cash Flow Signals, alongside declining cash flow and excessive withdrawals. The other categories concern the business's operations, the broader economy, and account-level activity respectively.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed under Rescheduling of Repayments as a Loan Workout Technique?
opts: Reducing the interest rate
Appointment of a Receiver Manager
Conversion of Import Finance Facility to Warehouse Finance
Write-off of a portion of the loan
questionBank.ans: Appointment of a Receiver Manager
questionBank.exp: Reducing the interest rate is listed under Rescheduling of Repayments, alongside amending the schedule to cash flow patterns and rescheduling due dates. The other options are listed under Loan Recovery Methods, Restructuring, and Administrative Effort respectively.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as an objective of the Basel Accords?
opts: Maximizing short-term shareholder dividends across all member banks
Strengthening financial soundness in banks
Eliminating the need for any bank capital requirements
Standardizing bank branding across jurisdictions
questionBank.ans: Strengthening financial soundness in banks
questionBank.exp: Strengthening financial soundness in banks is a listed Basel Accord objective, alongside introducing strong risk management practices and ensuring global consistency of application. The other options are not listed objectives.

questionBank.q: What does Tier 3 capital consist of, according to the material?
opts: Equity and disclosed reserves
Short-term Subordinated Debt
Undisclosed and revaluation reserves
General provisions and hybrid instruments
questionBank.ans: Short-term Subordinated Debt
questionBank.exp: Tier 3 consists of Short-term Subordinated Debt. The other options describe Tier 1 (equity and disclosed reserves) and components of Tier 2 (undisclosed/revaluation reserves, general provisions, hybrid instruments) instead.

questionBank.q: How do Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital respectively differ in composition and in the limit placed on Tier 2?
opts: Tier 1 is supplementary capital with no limit; Tier 2 is core capital limited to 50% of Tier 1
Tier 1 is core capital (equity and disclosed reserves); Tier 2 is supplementary capital, limited to 100% of Tier 1
Tier 1 and Tier 2 are identical in composition, with no limit on either
Tier 1 is core capital limited to 100% of Tier 2; Tier 2 is supplementary capital with no limit
questionBank.ans: Tier 1 is core capital (equity and disclosed reserves); Tier 2 is supplementary capital, limited to 100% of Tier 1
questionBank.exp: Tier 1 is core capital made up of equity and disclosed reserves; Tier 2 is supplementary capital (undisclosed/revaluation reserves, general provisions, hybrid instruments, subordinated debt), limited to 100% of Tier 1. The other options reverse or misstate this relationship.
